Midnight hypotheses

Florence, January. Giulia has received an email from Malta: she is invited to lead the restoration of Caravaggio's "Beheading of Saint John the Baptist" in Valletta for six months. It's midnight. She and Matei can't sleep.
Are you asleep?
No. I'm thinking about Malta. If we said yes, when would we leave?
In March. Until September. Assuming the workshop can manage without us for six months.
Chiara would manage. She proved it with the banner. Provided she wants to, of course.
And Viola? Should she fall ill in Malta, far from everyone…
There are hospitals in Malta, Giulia. And in case of problems, Florence is an hour and a half away by plane.
And what if we said no? Supposing we never get a Caravaggio like this again?
Then in twenty years we'd say: "If we'd known, we'd have gone."
"Se lo sapevamo, ci andavamo"? Matei, that's bar-room Italian.
I know. But at two in the morning the congiuntivo trapassato won't come to me. If you like, I can say: "Se l'avessimo saputo, ci saremmo andati."
Better. And if by any chance we decided to go, who's going to tell Graziella?
That, my love, is the only hypothesis that really scares me.

"Nel caso in cui" is less formal than "qualora", which you saw in chapter 53. "In caso di pioggia" is typical on posters and invitations.
2. Ammesso che, supponendo che, posto che
All of them introduce a hypothesis accepted "for the moment" in order to reason further. All take the congiuntivo:
ammesso che
Ammesso che Chiara accetti, chi la aiuterebbe?
I grant that, but…
supponendo che
Supponendo che il volo costi poco, verrebbero tutti.
let's suppose
posto che
Posto che lei voglia, naturalmente.
provided (implicitly) that
ammesso e non concesso che
Ammesso e non concesso che tu abbia ragione…
I grant it only for the sake of argument
"Ammesso e non concesso" is a debating formula: "let's say you're right, though I don't think so".
3. Se dovesse + infinitive
"Dovere" in the congiuntivo imperfetto + infinitive makes the hypothesis less likely, like English "should it happen that…":
Se dovesse piovere, la festa si farebbe dentro.
Se dovessi perderti, chiamami.
Should you get lost, call me.
Se dovesse ammalarsi, torneremmo subito.
Should she fall ill, we'd come back at once.
In the main clause you can have the conditional (torneremmo) or even the imperative (chiamami) or the present (ti chiamo), because the hypothesis is possible.
4. Casomai, volendo, the hypothetical gerund
casomai / semmai + cong.
Casomai decidessimo di andare, chi lo dice a Graziella?
casomai (on its own)
Porta l’ombrello, casomai.
volendo
Volendo, potremmo andare tutti.
if we want
Avendo più tempo, verrei anch’io.
= se avessi più tempo
The hypothetical gerund is elegant and short: "Potendo, partirei domani" = If I could, I'd leave tomorrow.
5. The colloquial hypothetical sentence
In everyday speech many Italians replace the impossible hypothetical sentence with two imperfetto indicatives:
Se mi chiamavi, ti aiutavo.
Se mi avessi chiamato, ti avrei aiutato.
You must RECOGNISE it, because you'll hear it everywhere. But in an exam, a letter or a speech use the standard form.
In case of problems, call me.

The standard version of "Se lo sapevo, venivo":
Se lo saprei, verrei.
Se lo sapessi, venivo.
"Avendo più tempo, verrei" means:
If I had more time, I'd come.
Because I have more time, I'm coming.
Although I have more time, I'm not coming.
"Porta l'ombrello, casomai" means:
Take the umbrella, just in case.
Take the umbrella, you might lose it.
Take the umbrella, it's a case.

La lettera da La Valletta

The email arrived on 7 January, the first working day after the holidays, while Giulia was still taking the Christmas decorations out of the workshop window. The sender was a Dr Joseph Camilleri, director of restoration at St John's Co-Cathedral in Valletta, Malta. Giulia read it once standing up, a second time sitting down and a third time aloud, because Matei, on the other side of the workshop, had asked her why she had gone so pale.

"Dear Dr Esposito," the email said, "we have followed with great interest your work on the Burial of Saint Lucy in Syracuse and the discovery of the so-called 'Totò'. As you will know, our Co-Cathedral houses the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, Caravaggio's largest work and the only one he signed. Should you be available, we would be honoured to entrust you with the direction of the new restoration, from March to September. Should you decide to accept, we would provide an apartment in Valletta for you and your family."

For a long moment neither of them spoke. Then Matei came over, read the email over Giulia's shoulder, and said only: "The only signed one." It was true. Caravaggio had written his name just once in his life, at the bottom of that painting, in the red of the saint's blood: "f. Michelang.o". Every restorer in the world dreamed of seeing that signature up close. And now someone was asking Giulia to look after it for six months.

That night they didn't sleep. They lay in bed with their eyes open, talking quietly so as not to wake Viola, building hypotheses one on top of another like a house of cards. If they said yes, who would run the workshop? Assuming Chiara accepted, who would help her? Should Viola fall ill in Malta, what would they do? And if they said no, supposing an opportunity like this never came again, would they forgive themselves? At two Matei fell asleep mid-sentence. Giulia stayed awake until dawn.

The next morning they decided not to tell anyone until they had decided. The decision lasted exactly until a quarter past nine, when Bellini, who now came to the workshop every morning "only for half a day, as the cardiologist says", walked in, looked at their faces and said: "What's happened? You look like two people who've found a Caravaggio under the bed." Giulia burst out laughing nervously. Then she let him read the email.

Bellini read it in silence, twice. Then he took off his glasses, cleaned them on his tie and said something neither of them expected. "In 1992," he said, "they called me from Malta for the same painting. I was twenty-eight. I said no, because I was afraid to leave my father's workshop, because I thought I wasn't up to it, because I didn't know anyone in Malta. I've thought about it for more than thirty years." He put his glasses back on. "Se lo sapevo, ci andavo," he said. Then he corrected himself with a half smile: "If I had known, I would have gone. Forgive me. When I talk about regrets, bar-room Italian comes out."

Then, in a lower voice, he told them the rest. In 1992 he had already bought the ferry ticket from Catania. He had packed his suitcase, his brushes, even a Maltese dictionary he never opened. The evening before he was due to leave, his father fell from the workshop ladder and broke his wrist. "Nobody asked me to stay," said Bellini. "My father actually told me to go. But I thought: should something else happen to him while I'm away, I'd never forgive myself. So I stayed. The wrist healed in six weeks. The regret, on the other hand, has never healed." He took from his wallet a yellowed ticket, folded in four: "Catania – Valletta, 14 March 1992". He had never thrown it away.

Giulia and Matei looked at each other. They hadn't known Bellini had been called to Malta. Nobody had known. "And now," Bellini went on, "you're asking my advice, even though you haven't asked. I'll give it anyway. Granting that the workshop needs you, and it does, it needs you to become the best even more. And the best, every so often, must leave. The workshop isn't going anywhere. I guarantee it, I who survived a heart attack to keep it open."

The next problem was Chiara. If Giulia and Matei left, someone would have to run the workshop for six months, with three restorations under way, Davide on Saturdays, the open workshop and a convalescent professor who wasn't supposed to lift anything heavier than a brush. They called her that very evening, at the trattoria. Chiara listened to everything without interrupting, eating her ribollita more and more slowly. At the end she put down her spoon. "Supposing I say yes," she said, "can I have an assistant?"

"An assistant?" asked Matei. "And where do we find an assistant in two months?" Chiara pointed with her chin at the next table, where Davide was doing his maths homework under Rita's stern gaze. "I've already got one," she said. "He's thirteen, he draws better than I do and he knows how to call an ambulance. If need be, Pietro can come on Saturdays as a guide. The other days I'll manage on my own. And in case of emergency, I'll call you in Malta. Or the professor. Or, should everything really go wrong, Signora Graziella."

Davide, from the next table, had heard everything. He abandoned his maths, despite Rita's look, and came to sit with them. "I'm in," he said at once, before anyone could ask him. "Assuming Mum agrees. And provided I can keep going to school, of course." Rita, from her table, rolled her eyes. "School is not negotiable," she said. "But if your marks stay good, you can go to the workshop in the afternoons. Should they drop, even by half a point, Chiara finds another assistant." Davide solemnly swore on the cartoon of the pot that his marks would go up. Chiara shook his hand as you do with a colleague. It was the first employment contract of his life, and they signed it, of course, on a napkin.

At that name a silence fell. Because there was still the last hypothesis, the most frightening of all: telling Graziella. Giulia and Matei had lived above the trattoria for four years. Viola had been born in that house, had taken her first steps on that floor, had said her first word at that table. Graziella cooked her baby food every lunchtime, sang her Florentine songs, took her to the Santo Spirito market like a holy relic. Six months without Viola, for Graziella, would be like six months without ribollita.

They decided to tell her on Sunday, at lunch, when the whole family was together. Matei prepared a speech. Giulia prepared another speech, shorter. Pietro, who had been told first because "he'll find out anyway", prepared a list of arguments in favour, numbered from one to seven, with the words "first of all" and "consequently". But when Graziella brought the roast to the table and sat down, nobody had the courage to begin. She spoke first, looking at them one by one.

"So," she said. "When are you leaving for Malta?" There was a deathly silence. Matei dropped his fork. "How… how do you know?" Graziella shrugged. "The professor said nothing, if that's what you think. But for a week you two have had the faces of people who have to leave, Pietro has been writing lists with the word 'consequently', and Chiara is counting assistants on a napkin. And then yesterday the postman brought a parcel marked 'Heritage' with a stamp showing the Maltese cross. I may be old, but I'm not stupid."

Giulia looked at Matei. Matei looked at Pietro. Pietro looked at his list, with seven numbered arguments that would no longer be needed. "And… what do you think?" Giulia asked softly. Graziella carved the roast calmly, served everyone, and only when she had finished did she answer. "I think that if I were to tell you not to go, I'd be a selfish old woman. And I think that if I told you to go with a smile, I'd be a liar." She paused. "So I'll tell you the truth. Go. But should the little one forget about ribollita, I'll come and fetch her myself. Swimming, if necessary."

Everyone laughed, but with wet eyes. Pietro, who didn't want to waste his work, read out the list of seven arguments anyway, "for the record", and the seventh made even Graziella laugh: "Consequently, in Malta they speak English and Italian, so Viola will become trilingual and will be able to teach Grandma English." Graziella replied that she didn't need English, because ribollita is understood in every language. Matei promised they would come back every month. Giulia promised every two weeks. Viola, from her high chair, promised "Figo", which nobody knew how to interpret.

But the decision hadn't been made yet. That evening Giulia wrote a reply to Dr Camilleri, deleted it, rewrote it and deleted it again. The problem was no longer "whether" but "how". If all three of them went, Viola would have to change nursery, habits, language. Supposing Matei stayed in Florence with her, the family would be split for six months. And assuming Giulia went alone, how could she work ten hours a day on a Caravaggio while thinking of a two-and-a-half-year-old a thousand kilometres away?

In the end it was Matei who found the right sentence, around midnight, while they were making camomile tea. "Giulia," he said, "we've spent a week building hypotheses. 'In case', 'assuming that', 'supposing that'. But a restorer doesn't decide on hypotheses. He decides by looking at the painting." Giulia looked at him without understanding. "Let's go and see it," Matei explained. "One weekend. All three of us. We look at the painting, we look at the city, we look at the apartment. And then we decide. With our eyes, not with the congiuntivo."

Giulia was silent for a moment, the cup in her hand. Then she smiled for the first time in a week, a real smile, without hypotheses. She opened the computer and wrote a new reply, short, which this time she didn't delete: "Dear Dr Camilleri, thank you for your offer, which honours me deeply. Before giving you a final answer, I would like to visit Valletta with my family. Should it be possible, we could come on the first weekend of February. Kind regards, Giulia Esposito."

She pressed "send" and closed the computer. Then she went into Viola's room, where the little girl was sleeping with her thumb in her mouth and her cloth bunny under her arm, and stopped in the doorway to look at her, next to the family's notches marked on the door frame. Matei joined her and put an arm around her shoulders. "Imagine," he said very quietly, "if one day she restores a Caravaggio. And we have to decide whether to let her go." Giulia laughed softly. "Should that happen," she replied, "I promise I won't use the congiuntivo. I'll just tell her: go."
